crop_profile.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a globally important annual cereal grown on loamy to clay soils with pH 6.0-7.5. Optimal temperatures are 10-25 °C, rainfall 300-900 mm/year, and sunlight 6-10 h/day. It requires medium water and nitrogen, with critical moisture needs during flowering. Major producers include China, India, Russia, the United States, and France. Typical yields are 3 t/ha, reaching up to 7 t/ha under optimal management. Key diseases are Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and leaf rust; main pests include aphids, Hessian fly, and wheat midge. Integrated pest management, split nitrogen fertilization, and timely harvest ensure high quality grain.

Record ambient temperature and humidity twice daily; watch for temperatures >30 °C.
Re‑capture NDVI (or use drone imagery) weekly to track vegetation recovery; target NDVI >0.45 within two weeks.
Re‑assess leaf nitrogen and carbon status after 10 days of organic amendment.

steps.finding: Perform an immediate field inspection, followed by targeted irrigation, disease/nutrient assessment, and organic soil amendment to mitigate heat and water stress.
actions: Inspect the wheat stand for signs of disease (e.g., Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew) and nutrient deficiencies; collect leaf and stem samples for lab analysis.
Start supplemental irrigation using surface or sprinkler systems to raise soil moisture to field capacity; apply water every 3–4 days during the critical flowering stage.
Apply well‑composted organic manure (e.g., 5 t/ha) to increase soil organic carbon and improve water‑holding capacity.
Lay a thin layer of mulch (straw or biodegradable film) around the rows to reduce evaporation and moderate soil temperature.
If disease is confirmed, treat with the appropriate fungicide (e.g., a registered product for Fusarium head blight) according to label rates.
steps.justification: Satellite data shows critical vegetation health (NDVI 0.154) and severe water stress, while temperatures are 30.5 °C, well above wheat's optimal range. Soil conditions are otherwise favorable (optimal pH, high nitrogen, suitable texture), but low organic carbon and lack of rainfall threaten yield. Prompt inspection and corrective actions are needed to prevent substantial yield loss.
